project.title: The Company That Sells You Nothing

frameZero.text: THE COMPANY THAT SELLS YOU NOTHING

sequences.openQuestion: How can a gym support this many members?
sequences.answer: The empty room is the contradiction: huge membership, limited physical capacity.

sequences.openQuestion: What if low attendance is not a failure?
sequences.answer: The business model benefits when members do not consume scarce capacity.

sequences.openQuestion: Why would friction be the product?
sequences.answer: The story moves from fitness to recurring-payment psychology.

sequences.openQuestion: How does a payment become background noise?
sequences.answer: $86 becomes $219 when consumers itemize; $133 is the perceptual gap.

sequences.openQuestion: Where did the pattern spread?
sequences.answer: The mechanism is portable across industries.

sequences.openQuestion: What kind of member creates the best economics?
sequences.answer: Capacity is the scarce resource; usage changes marginal service cost.

sequences.openQuestion: How is subscription breakage different from a gift card?
sequences.answer: The mechanism gets a name: BREAKAGE.

sequences.openQuestion: What does recurring forgetting become?
sequences.answer: A one-time break becomes a recurring stream of revenue.

sequences.openQuestion: Why did the contract become a liability?
sequences.answer: A visible contract creates a visible dispute and an identifiable complaint.

sequences.openQuestion: What replaces the visible contract?
sequences.answer: The visible weapon disappears; friction becomes the replacement.

sequences.openQuestion: Can a low price make leaving feel irrational?
sequences.answer: Low price plus friction can replace long contracts.

sequences.openQuestion: Why can stopping feel more expensive than continuing?
sequences.answer: Time and attention become hidden cancellation costs.

sequences.openQuestion: What happens when software applies the same model to ownership?
sequences.answer: The gym is selling an intention gap, not only access.

sequences.openQuestion: What happens when a one-time purchase becomes a recurring relationship?
sequences.answer: The subscription idea migrates from gym access into owned software.

sequences.openQuestion: Why is one-time ownership a problem for Adobe?
sequences.answer: A product can remain excellent while the upgrade cycle leaves revenue waiting.

sequences.openQuestion: What if the product itself stops being a one-time purchase?
sequences.answer: Creative Suite ends; Creative Cloud becomes the continuing relationship.

sequences.openQuestion: How did customers react to ownership being replaced?
sequences.answer: The backlash is evidence that the economic relationship changed for the customer too.

sequences.openQuestion: Did the subscription model actually change the economics?
sequences.answer: Adobe subscription revenue grows from the historical 2013 base to much larger modern recurring revenue.

sequences.openQuestion: Where else did the model spread?
sequences.answer: Streaming provides a larger consumer proof point.

sequences.openQuestion: Why did streaming feel like an escape from cable?
sequences.answer: The original promise was pay-for-what-you-want flexibility.

sequences.openQuestion: What happens when every studio wants its own relationship with the customer?
sequences.answer: The catalogue fragments and more subscription decisions appear.

sequences.openQuestion: Did streaming rebuild the bundle?
sequences.answer: Many small recurring charges recreate the logic of one large recurring bill.

sequences.openQuestion: What matters most once the subscription is easy to start?
sequences.answer: The exit becomes the most revealing part of the system.

sequences.openQuestion: What did regulators allege about the entrance to Prime?
sequences.answer: The investigation moves from business economics into interface behavior.

sequences.openQuestion: What happens when cancellation is designed as a sequence instead of a button?
sequences.answer: Each retention step increases the effort required to leave.

sequences.openQuestion: What did insiders call the cancellation sequence?
sequences.answer: Iliad — an understated but powerful name for a long cancellation journey.

sequences.openQuestion: How consequential did the case become?
sequences.answer: $2.5B settlement: $1B civil penalty plus $1.5B refunds.

sequences.openQuestion: Was Amazon unique?
sequences.answer: Adobe faces a separate cancellation case; the mechanism appears across industries.

sequences.openQuestion: Would a federal rule finally solve the exit problem?
sequences.answer: Click-to-Cancel promises symmetry between entry and exit.

sequences.openQuestion: What happens to the fix when it is challenged?
sequences.answer: The federal rule is vacated before enforcement begins.

sequences.openQuestion: Why did the rule fail?
sequences.answer: The court's ruling turns on regulatory procedure, not an endorsement of deceptive design.

sequences.openQuestion: What is the legal situation now?
sequences.answer: No nationwide federal Click-to-Cancel rule is currently in force; other laws may still apply.

sequences.openQuestion: Why does the empty gym still matter?
sequences.answer: The economics are not only about fitness; they are about attention and inertia.

sequences.openQuestion: What did the opening image actually mean?
sequences.answer: The empty gym is no longer a mystery; it is evidence of the business logic.

sequences.openQuestion: What link did subscriptions weaken?
sequences.answer: Payment can continue after active consumption stops.

sequences.openQuestion: What should the $133 figure actually mean?
sequences.answer: It is a measured perception gap, not a claim that everyone wastes exactly $133.

sequences.openQuestion: What can the viewer do right now?
sequences.answer: Audit twelve months of recurring charges and turn silent renewals back into explicit choices.

sequences.openQuestion: What is the real choice underneath the whole story?
sequences.answer: A subscription should remain a deliberate choice, not an unnoticed agreement that keeps running.

sequences.openQuestion: Where did the model spread?
sequences.answer: Cars, printers, doorbells, appliances — features in things you own. Making it hard to leave is the product.

sequences.openQuestion: What was the FTC's case about?
sequences.answer: Enrollment without understanding — dark patterns: the expensive choice is the easy one.

sequences.openQuestion: How many people were affected?
sequences.answer: Millions paying for a subscription they never knowingly started — but the famous part was cancelling.

sequences.openQuestion: What did Amazon employees call it?
sequences.answer: Iliad — a name for the sequence that would not end.

sequences.openQuestion: Why the name Iliad?
sequences.answer: Somebody inside Amazon saw a path that famously would not end — and they kept it.

sequences.openQuestion: How did the case end?
sequences.answer: Mid-trial, Amazon settled.

sequences.openQuestion: What was the hidden fee?
sequences.answer: Half of the remaining contract — month four, leaving cost half of eight months. Adobe paid $75M.

sequences.openQuestion: What did both cases share?
sequences.answer: Two of the largest companies, penalised within two years, for making it hard to stop paying.

sequences.openQuestion: If the cases win, what next?
sequences.answer: The obvious question — and somebody did.

sequences.openQuestion: What did click-to-cancel demand?
sequences.answer: Symmetry: whatever effort to begin, no more to end.

sequences.openQuestion: Who opposed the rule?
sequences.answer: Companies and the largest trade associations fought it hard.

sequences.openQuestion: What happened days before the rule took effect?
sequences.answer: The Eighth Circuit struck it down. Entirely.

sequences.openQuestion: Did the court reject the rule's substance?
sequences.answer: No — the FTC failed to carry out a required preliminary regulatory analysis.

sequences.openQuestion: What killed the rule?
sequences.answer: A paperwork failure — years of rulemaking vacated days before the deadline.

sequences.openQuestion: What is the status in 2026?
sequences.answer: No federal click-to-cancel rule in effect; FTC restarting; states have their own laws.

sequences.openQuestion: Is this an oversight?
sequences.answer: A deliberate, documented, profitable design — reviewed, and left in place.

sequences.openQuestion: Why return to the empty gym?
sequences.answer: The business works because the people paying are not there.

sequences.openQuestion: What kept old business honest?
sequences.answer: If it stopped delivering, you stopped paying — that link was the discipline.

sequences.openQuestion: What did subscriptions break?
sequences.answer: The payment continues on its own until you act — action the company makes harder than you can be bothered with.

sequences.openQuestion: What is the $133 gap really?
sequences.answer: The measured output of a system built to convert attention into revenue.

sequences.openQuestion: What can you do with this?
sequences.answer: Search twelve months of statements for same-amount, same-date charges.

sequences.openQuestion: Do you have to cancel everything?
sequences.answer: Some you'll keep — that's fine. That's a choice.
It should be a choice — right now it's just the last thing you agreed to, still running.
